<reason>B won by making the decisive clash easier to judge: social-graph transfer is other people’s associations, not the user’s suitcase. A had a strong lock-in/exit-threat case and a clever reconnection design, but kept narrowing the motion into hashed pointers, after-the-fact prompts, and carve-outs. B answered that the map still leaves first, exclusions rewrite or leave sensitive lock-in, and refusing this instrument is not “no remedy.” Ownership beat A’s default-win-on-lock-in frame.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s R1–R2 attack on A’s reconnection design: a prompt is not prior consent, the compelled graph still leaves, and filtering blocked users/minors either dumps sensitive ties or preserves the lock-in the mandate claims to cure.</best_rebuttal>
